thread.title: Dow Gains 150 Points as Fear Fades, Despite Rising Bond Yields

author: Ben Levisohn
title: Dow Gains 150 Points as Fear Fades, Despite Rising Bond Yields
text:
Stocks, which had looked primed for a selloff this morning , have bounced back in a big way even as Treasury yields rise. But should we still be afraid there's more pain to come?
Illustration: Getty Images Sure, the S&P 500 has risen 0.4% to 2834.72 at 12:22 p.m. today, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average has gained 149.48 points, or 0.6%, to 26,298.87. The Nasdaq Composite has risen 0.3%, to 7430.28. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen 0.03 percentage point to 2.75%.
So bond yields don't seem to be a problem today. But what about tomorrow? Albert Edwards, Société Générale's resident permabear, thinks we should—even if he doesn't believe the bond bull market is over. "With the U.S. 10-year yield breaking above its long-term downtrend, equity prices have begun to wobble," he says. "Although I agree with the bond bears that U.S. yields will continue to rise, causing more problems for equities, I do not believe bond yields have yet seen a secular bottom. I repeat my forecast that U.S. 10-year yields will fall below zero."
Now that's frightening. But frightening enough to make investors head for the exits? My expectation is that rising yields will lead to more volatility , but not end the bull market...
...at least not yet.
Textron: Bouncing Back What a difference a day makes for Textron (TXT).
Shares of Textron, whose products include Cessna business jets and Bell helicopters, fell 2.5% yesterday following the company's fourth-quarter earnings release, which included disappointing guidance . But its shares are recovering today after Morgan Stanley analyst Rajeev Lalwani upgraded its shares to Equal Weight from Underweight.
"The weak [guidance] pushed shares down 2%-3%, while peers were largely up on the day,” notes Lalwani. He upgraded the stock, however, partly owing to the “growing probability of a [business] jet recovery.”
The business-jet market, which has been sluggish in recent years partly owing to a glut of used aircraft, has showed some signs of recovering recently. When Barron’s wrote about the market last fall, we were skeptical about the stock, which looked pricey at the time (“ Ready to Fly High Again ,” Sept. 30, 2017). It still does: It trades at about 19.4 times the $3.05 analysts expect it to earn this year, at the higher end of its valuation range over the past five years, according to FactSet.
Shares of Textron have gained 2.4%, to $60.06, at 11:45 a.m. today. The stock has returned around 27% in the past year, slightly ahead of the S&P 500. — Lawrence C. Strauss
Asia Tech: Time to Shine? By the end of today, most big U.S. tech companies— Facebook (FB), Microsoft (MSFT), Apple (AAPL), Amazon.com (AMZN), and Alphabet (GOOGL), among them—will have reported earnings. And from the looks of it, many investors expect tech stocks to keep on doing what they've been doing...leading the market higher.
Illustration: Getty Images Not everyone is enthusiastic, however. In a report this morning, the strategists at Pavilion Global Markets recommended investors look to Asia for their tech ideas. Part of the reason is valuation. Many investors take solace in the fact that the valuations of U.S. tech stocks are in line with the overall market, unlike during the tech bubble, when the sector traded at a hefty premium.
Pavilion, though, notes that unlike 2000, the entire U.S. market is expensive now. "The issue here is that Growth stocks and Value stocks are both expensive relative to their historical valuations," the strategists write.
Asian tech companies, however, are trading at a discount to U.S. ones , and also have more growth opportunities. Tencent Holdings (0700.Hong Kong) gets just 5% of its revenue from foreign sources, Pavilion says, while Alibaba Group Holding (BABA) gets 24%. That compares to 58% for Apple and 53% for Alphabet. "We believe the tide will slowly be turning to a greater deal of Tech revenues being attributed to Asian firms from domestic and foreign sources,” Pavilion says.
Would that make Alibaba's earnings-driven selloff today a buying opportunity? — B.L.
Chevron Hikes Its Dividend In a preamble to its earnings report tomorrow, Chevron (CVX) raised its dividend for the first time since 2016.
Chevron declared a quarterly dividend of $1.12 a share, up 4% from $1.08. It marked the first announced dividend hike for the major oil company since October 2016, when it raised its dividend from $1.07 to $1.08, a less than 1% increase. So while the most recent hike isn't huge, it's much larger than its previous one. The stock was yielding about 3.6%.
Unfortunately, the dividend hike has done nothing to halt Chevron's recent slide. Its shares have dropped 0.8% to $124.34 at 11:22 a.m. today, putting it down more than 5% this week, while the Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE) has fallen 0.2%, to $74.67.
Maybe Chevron's earnings can do what the dividend couldn't. — L.C.S.
